_about: The war plan (after release 1; off by default, and off the game is release 1's move for move). A computer staff that thinks a season ahead. Month by month a staff weighs each front and attacks where the whole front's strength ratio is good enough (open.json). That leaves three gaps a thoughtful commander would not: a front at even strength sleeps for years because nobody gathers the army at one place; an enemy foothold on the coast is watched and never thrown back; and reserves answer only the enemy standing next door. With 'on' true, at the dial's 'stops' (the two where anything goes: at stop 3, in 24 wars with every staff planning, Germany fell a middle of four months sooner, which par at that stop does not allow until the design director rules on it), the staffs named in 'staffs' (empty: every computer-run nation with a staff character) plan campaigns. 'campaign': when the staff has attacked 'few' times or fewer in 'quiet' months on a front (a front gone quiet), a front whose ratio is at least 'ratio'[0] (under it the staff is on the strategic defensive) and under 'ratio'[1] (over it the ordinary offensive does the work), a staff that leads there (it has 'least' corps of its own fit to mass on the front, and they are the share 'own' or more of all its side has on it: a small ally on a greater army's front makes no plan of its own) picks the enemy province where the force it could gather (the best corps the roads into it can carry, tanks and guns first, from 'reach' marches around) would go in at 'strike' odds or better by the staff's own sums, weighing the road beyond it ('road' for the first province of the easiest road to his capital, 'beside' for its neighbours, less the going and 'works' for fortifications). It spends 'prep' months ([fewest, most]) massing: 'tanks' fast corps and infantry up to 'doors' at each of up to 'most' provinces next to the target, the rest of the line keeping what it needs. When the massed force has 'go' odds at the target by the battle's own reckoning the blow falls and is pressed for 'push' months whatever the front's ratio, as a general offensive along the road that starts where the army stands; if 'prep'[1] months pass without those odds the plan is dropped. After a campaign the front rests 'rest' months. 'foothold': an enemy piece of ground of 'size' provinces or fewer on this staff's own side's ground, with the sea behind it, is thrown back before it grows: where the staff's own sums give the force it can bring 'go' odds, and no other front with a real army on it stands under the ratio 'safe', it masses against it at once, whatever else it is doing ('tanks' fast corps and infantry up to 'doors' at each of up to 'most' provinces beside it), strikes at 'go' odds and presses for 'push' months; it keeps at it while the foothold has 'grown' provinces or fewer, after which it is a front like any other. 'recall' (its own 'on' is false: built, measured and left off. In 24 wars with it Italy left the war a middle of four months later than without, and Germany fell no sooner: the corps called out of Africa, home or to the camp of the army abroad on the island it had just taken, were the ones whose next steps, Crete and then Sardinia or Sicily, put Italy out; and the home army was never short of men for France, only of a place to put them ashore. It waits for the design director's form of 'the need ends and the corps go where the next need is'): an army that has won its theatre goes back into the war. An army standing on friendly ground across the water, in one piece away from home, with no enemy on that ground or next to it (nor an enemy's ally, at war yet or not: Italy in Libya in 1939) and no battle on it or beside it for 'quiet' months, keeps a guard (one corps for each harbour of that ground an enemy's troopships can still reach, no fewer than 'least' (nor than a landing force, open.json 'descent.force', so that the ground stays a quay its army abroad can name for its next step) and no more than 'most', the weakest of them; the corps an order holds in place stay besides, and so does the landing force of the army abroad: the corps at its quay and, where 'landing.waves' is set, the waves it counts on, the best within those marches of the quay, as many as a first wave and the ships' months after it; and nobody is called from the homeland across a strait) and sends the rest, the strongest first, with the shipping left after the month's landings: into a harbour of a front its side holds across the water (its own landing first), where the test of strength lets a corps in; or home, to the landing quay; over no crossing riskier than 'risk', and from the harbours of Egypt round the Cape where the Mediterranean is too dangerous, the way they came (middle-east.json). While the army abroad's landing force is short of that count, the corps sent gather to it first: by sea into a harbour within those marches of its quay, or by road to the quay where the roads join. Those not in a harbour march to the nearest one with a way out. Not for a staff whose army goes by the ocean runs. 'landing': with 'second' true, a staff whose men ashore are still too few but whose every harbour there is full, so that no ship can bring another corps, lands its next wave on a harbour beside the ground they hold, that month, with no wait and no dice, under every test of a landing; where before it waited. 'waves': a planning staff reckons an invasion as a campaign, in place of the test of strength as ruled (open.json 'descent.strength'), on the same count of strength and against the same chance. The test as ruled counts one place and what five corps can hold there, so a staff with twenty corps free at home waited until five would do. A planning staff counts, behind a first wave as big as its ships lift (the quay is filled for it), the waves that follow in the months that are left: its fit corps free on quiet ground within 'within' marches of the quay, as many as the ships carry in those months and the floor at home lets go, at 'share' of their strength (not every wave finds room ashore on its day), where the place has another harbour of an enemy's beside it to land them on. And it counts the enemy's reply: his reserves out of the line 'reply' times over, for a staff that plans rails all it has free to a foothold at once ('foothold'). It feeds a foothold on the same reckoning it landed on; and while its men ashore are too few, the quay it feeds them from draws 'tanks' of its fast corps at a time as well as infantry (a foothold breaks out with tanks). And it builds the ships for it: with a landing in view and an army waiting on ships (more of the corps it counts on for its waves than its shipping, built and building, lifts in a month), it lays down troopships from the arsenal, one lot a month, at the player's price and above its reserve, within what the yards can take (arsenal.json 'lift'), until its shipping lifts 'ships' corps a month (two harbours' worth). Before, no computer staff ever laid one down.
